metadata.title: Steven Pinker vs Ross Douthat: Do We Need God?
metadata.label: Religion, secularism, and human flourishing
metadata.motion: Are people and societies better off with belief in God, or can secular reason and institutions provide morality, purpose, and social cooperation more effectively?
metadata.sourceNote: Assessment based exclusively on the complete locally cached YouTube caption transcript and timestamped events (transcript SHA-256 f8157f92111be5a6f01df90a0135f91fe39a0aac92b600dedd2d30a28313cd33). Required below-high-confidence audio checks were completed before adjudication; representative quotations must be exact strings from quote-eligible locked source spans.
metadata.scoringNote: Scores are AI-generated estimates of argumentative performance under the locked adjudicated-consensus workflow. Repository code calculated every move, section, and overall result once, only after two isolated judgments, required audio review, and disputed-field adjudication closed.

routes.description: Establish that belief in God supplies truth-grounded moral authority, purpose, human significance, and durable social commitments that secular reason and institutions cannot fully reproduce.
routes.successCriteria: Connect a credible transcendent account of reality to distinctive moral and social benefits, while showing that secular substitutes leave material gaps in obligation, meaning, solidarity, or confidence in humanity's future.

motionBridge.description: Show that the distinctive truth, moral, purposive, and communal functions of belief in God make people and societies better off overall.

centralBridges.description: Establish that morality requires a standard beyond prevailing consensus or self-interest to ground equal worth, prophetic criticism, and restraint of power.
Establish that a divinely ordered reality provides warranted purpose, human significance, and confidence in a shared future beyond material utility.
Establish that religious belief sustains forms of community and institutional commitment that secular civic or governmental substitutes do not fully preserve.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why inherited belief, religious disagreement, and scientific revision do not preclude rational commitment to fundamental religious truth claims.
Identify limits or tensions in naturalistic accounts of reason, consciousness, moral knowledge, and humanity's distinctive intellectual capacities.

routes.description: Establish that reason centered on human flourishing can ground morality, knowledge, purpose, and cooperation, while secular institutions can preserve beneficial social practices without theological commitments.
routes.successCriteria: Provide workable secular foundations for moral obligation and reliable knowledge, connect them to effective institutions and historical progress, and show that religion's beneficial components are separable from disputed doctrines.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular reason and institutions can provide morality, purpose, knowledge, and social cooperation at least as effectively without requiring belief in God.

centralBridges.description: Ground moral duties and equal rights in impartial consistency, reciprocal concern, conscious interests, agency, and the shared gains from cooperative conduct.
Establish empirical testing, correction, and information-processing explanations as sufficient foundations for reliable knowledge without supernatural premises.
Establish that public welfare, civic association, democracy, and universal human-rights institutions can deliver cooperation and moral progress at broad scale.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate religion's community, ritual, music, and fellowship from theological, repressive, or obsolete claims so beneficial practices can be retained selectively.
Require causal evidence before attributing well-being, cohesion, polarization, or historical violence to either religious belief or secularization.

sections.title: Foundations of morality, obligation, and equal worth
sections.rationale: The motion centrally turns on whether transcendent authority is needed to justify duties, protect equal human value, criticize accepted injustice, and restrain conduct that benefits powerful actors.

sections.title: Community, welfare, and institutional cooperation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether religion provides distinctive and durable social attachment or whether civic organizations, public programs, and selectively preserved communal practices can perform the relevant functions.

sections.title: Reason, religious truth, and naturalistic explanation
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of reliable knowledge determine whether belief in God is rationally warranted and whether evolution, scientific correction, cognition, and consciousness can be explained within a secular framework.

sections.title: Historical violence, institutional failure, and moral progress
sections.rationale: Claims about totalitarianism, religious complicity, institutional recovery, democracy, and human rights bear on which worldview can support stable improvement rather than merely inherit or cause social failures.

sections.title: Purpose, human significance, and confidence in the future
sections.rationale: The debate also requires comparing the resources of theistic and secular worldviews for sustaining personal meaning, human distinctiveness, social hope, and commitment to future generations.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling God's existence self-evident and linking religious decline to broad social maladies asserts substantially more than the excerpt's compressed support establishes.
